newsitem.title: HONG KONG: S&P sees Thai banks' bad loans peaking in '98.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees Thai banks' bad loans peaking in '98.

text.p: Standard and Poor's Corp expects Thai commercial banks' non-performing loan problems to peak in 1998, S&P said in a conference call on Friday.
"We do not expect to see the peak in the non-performing loan problem until well into 1998," said Peter Sikora, banking analyst with S&P in Melbourne.

S&P also said it expects commercial banks' percentage of non-performing loans to peak at 12-15 percent, which it said was higher than Thai government estimates. S&P's estimate also exceeds market expectations, S&P said.
The rating agency pointed out the banks' non-performing loan percentage was 7.7 percent at June 30, 1996, and appears to have risen to the "double digits" at the end of fiscal year 1996.
"The market expects the bad loan percentage to go up just an extra few hundred basis points, but we think it will be higher," said Sikora.
He said it is "very difficult to tell" to what extent the financial services sector outside of the commercial banks is exposed to bad loans, but the exposure is likely to be high.
Companies' bad loan problems will vary by industry, with those most exposed to the property sector most at risk, S&P said.

Recent measures by the government to shore up the financial sector through various measures, including the bestowing of incentives for troubled firms to merge, were "positive" developments and not just cosmetic changes, S&P said.
In an earlier conference call today, S&P said that the measures may not be sufficient to contain the problems within the property sector, however.
A weaker baht would, on balance, ease pressures on Thai banks, S&P said.

"A devaluation or a depreciation would ease credit conditions for those banks leveraged in baht terms while it would hurt banks with foreign exposure," said David Beers, S&P sovereign analyst in New York.
But S&P reiterated that it does not expect the Bank of Thailand to devalue the baht.
Asked if the baht exchange rate was appropriate, S&P was circumspect.
"The exchange rate is consistent with an economy that is in an adjustment period," an S&P sovereign analyst said.
While acknowledging that the Thai economy is in "disequilibrium," he said the exchange rate is correctly valued because the central bank is committed to the current exchange rate regime.

The baht rate is consistent with the government's desire to slow the economy and lower inflation, he said. Moreover, the current account deficit is narrowing without any efforts to weaken the currency, he said.
S&P expects Thailand's current account deficit to shrink to five percent of gross domestic product by next year, a forecast it deemed conservative.
S&P said it expects Thailand's short-term interest rates to stay relatively high until next year.
S&P affirmed Thailand's sovereign ratings and stable outlook last month. S&P rates Thailand's long-term foreign currency debt at Single-A and its long-term local currency debt at AA.

S&P reiterated in the conference call held earlier today that it does not believe that the troubles plaguing Thailand's financial sector will adversely affect the country's long-term sovereign rating because the problems are manageable.
